pull.title: KAFKA-21031: Another busy loop happens while a heartbeat is in flight and the heartbeat timer is expired
pull.body:
When a heartbeat response takes longer than the heartbeat interval, the
heartbeat timer expires while the request is still in flight. In that
case timeToNextHeartbeatMs() returns the remaining backoff, which is
measured from the last response and is usually already 0, so the
network and application threads busy loop until the response arrives
or the request times out. Return the retry backoff instead.

KAFKA-19804 (#23687) avoided this for the first heartbeat by starting
with request.timeout.ms as the interval; this covers the later ones.

Related: KAFKA-20253 (#22836), KAFKA-20970 (#23227), KAFKA-21010 (#23348).

Generated-by: OpenAI Codex, Anthropic Claude Opus

Reviewers: Doyeon Kim (@dybyte), Lianet Magrans
 <lmagrans@confluent.io>

repo.name: kafka
repo.description: Apache Kafka - A distributed event streaming platform

reviews.body:
This made me wonder about two similar paths:
`FetchRequestManager.maximumTimeToWait()` and the retry-backoff bounds in
`AsyncKafkaConsumer.pollForFetches()`.

When `retry.backoff.ms` is 0, both can also result in a zero
application-thread wait. Do you think the same floor should apply there,
or is that case intentional?

review_comments.body: is this comment needed or could we remove? seems like it can easily become stale if we make any changes to the implementation.
why only for hb interval > 0? `onSuccessfulAttempt` happens when we send , not when we receive the response (so I expect it's right to call it no matter the HB interval we have here?)
this comment is a bit confusing too, as `onSuccessfulAttempt` happens when we send (maybe remove if my other comment makes sense and we end up calling this regardless of the interval

uhm do we really need this test? We're unit testing the req manager and we already tested the in-flight case above, but seems this test is to cover the same case but going beyond to the other component (network client)? If so I would say we shouldn't get there and remove this?

if my [comment above](https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/23357/changes#r4037628360)  mnakes sense we need to update here too.

Actually maybe helpful to encapsulate the 2 assertion blocks (the 2 tests generate different scenarios but have the same expectations timeToNextPoll, ln 552-557 here and maximumTimeToWait, ln 544-550 right?)

+    /**
+     * Lower bound for the wait returned while a heartbeat is in flight. retry.backoff.ms and

review_comments.body:
I get the point with this, but it introduces an inconsistency, so I would say we either fix consistently (all req managers) or don't (we haven't used any floor in any of the other paths fixed IIRC)

`retry.backoff.ms=0` would be a very extreme/unexpected config setting I expect, so I wouldn't rush in any extra logic/complexity in the managers to guard against it, wdyt? We can always file something to review if it's worth any change but address it consistently

could we simplify this long comment? 

Probably ok to just highlight the "why" (timer can be expired while in-flight, and remaining backoff can be already 0, measured from the last response), so we return backoff to check again after a bit and avoid busy-spin)

> it can easily become stale if we make any changes to the implementation.

Agreed, done, next time I will avoid these type of comments.

`onSendAttempt()` is called when the heartbeat request is generated.

For heartbeats, `onSuccessfulAttempt()` is called when a successful response is received. The interval comes from that response, so the non-zero case simulates a previous successful response. The zero case represents the first heartbeat still awaiting its response.

I've simplified the comment to explain the prior successful response being simulated and removed the backoff detail. As noted in the other thread, `onSuccessfulAttempt()` is called on a successful response, while `onSendAttempt()` is called when the request is generated.
Agreed, removed the test and its dedicated helpers.

Re-open because this is not related to KIP-909, can verify it separately, c.c. @chia7712

> This made me wonder about two similar paths: `FetchRequestManager.maximumTimeToWait()` and the retry-backoff bounds in `AsyncKafkaConsumer.pollForFetches()`.
> 
> When `retry.backoff.ms` is 0, both can also result in a zero application-thread wait. Do you think the same floor should apply there, or is that case intentional?

Good catch. I do not think the zero wait is intentional.

In both paths, `retry.backoff.ms` is used as a bound while the application thread is waiting for background progress; it does not mean that useful work is immediately available. If it is configured as 0, `FetchRequestManager.maximumTimeToWait()` can feed 0 directly into `pollForFetches()`, and the state-based clamps inside `pollForFetches()` can also reduce a positive timeout to 0. `fetchBuffer.awaitWakeup()` then returns immediately and the outer poll loop can repeat without progress.

So in my opinion, the same positive floor seems appropriate. It would be good to keep it separate from this PR, though: this change is specifically about the heart-beat path.

@lianetm KAFKA-19804 (#23687) is now on trunk and already covers the first
heartbeat, so I dropped that case and the dedicated tests. The wait is now
asserted at the end of your testHeartbeatNotSentIfAnotherOneInFlight (from
KAFKA-16528), where the next heartbeat stays in flight past the interval,
plus a small HeartbeatRequestStateTest case.

@frankvicky Could you also take a look since you reviewed #23687 ? This covers the
later heartbeats that #23687 does not, thanks !

commit.message:
KAFKA-21031: Add tests for the busy loop while a heartbeat is in flight

The heartbeat timer is reset when a heartbeat is sent. If it is expired
while the request is still in flight, timeToNextHeartbeatMs() returns 0,
and the heartbeat managers use that value both as the network poll timeout
and in maximumTimeToWait(), so both threads spin until the response or a
failure arrives. This happens for the first heartbeat of a consumer
instance (the interval is initialised to 0 and only known from the first
response) and for any later heartbeat whose response is slower than the
interval.

The tests cover both cases with a parameterised heartbeat interval of 0
and 5000 for the state object and for the consumer, share and streams
heartbeat managers, a zero retry backoff on the state object, a consumer
manager test where the interval is learned from a real heartbeat response
and the next heartbeat's response is slower than that interval, and a test
with a real NetworkClient on a MockSelector where the heartbeat is sent
and never answered. That test drives the network poll with the manager's
own wait time, so the mock clock only moves when the wait is positive,
and it bounds the number of polls while the request is in flight; it also
checks that the request times out and a second heartbeat is sent. They
fail on trunk and pass with the fix.

Generated-by: Claude Fable 5.1

KAFKA-21031: Do not busy-spin while a heartbeat is in flight and the timer is expired

HeartbeatRequestState resets the heartbeat timer when a heartbeat is sent.
While that request is in flight the manager cannot send another one, so
poll() and maximumTimeToWait() fall back to timeToNextHeartbeatMs(). If the
timer is expired at that point, it returns remainingBackoffMs(), which is
measured from the last response and, with default settings, is already 0. The heartbeat
managers use that 0 as the network poll timeout and as the application
thread wait, so both threads spin until the response or a failure arrives.

The timer is expired while a request is in flight in two cases:

- the first heartbeat of a consumer instance, because the interval is
  initialised to 0 and only known from the first response; with an
  unreachable coordinator this repeats every request.timeout.ms;
- any later heartbeat whose response takes longer than the interval, for
  example a coordinator in a long GC pause.

In both cases nothing can be sent until the in-flight request completes,
so return the effective initial retry backoff, floored at 1 ms, and check
again, the same way the coordinator-unknown guard waits. The floor is
needed because retry.backoff.ms and retry.backoff.max.ms both accept 0 and
callers use this value as a poll timeout. Waiting forever is not safe here: the
network client only notices a timed-out request after its poll returns,
and the network thread caps that poll at five seconds, so a heartbeat
that hits request.timeout.ms would be noticed late.
